323.title: The emperor on the langar floor
323.hook: the first visit: a Sikh kitchen where even an emperor sat on the floor
323.carry: seva: everyone eats at the same height
323.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Buddhist means by the breath
323.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, sweeping, and caring for shoes, and outside it through relief work; the langar serves a free meal to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor.

segments.voice: Yesterday the three tracks ended: karma, bhakti, jnana. Serving, singing, asking, and all of them a doing. This week you visit the neighbors, one house a day, and Priya's class goes with you.

Shoes off. Head covered. Hands washed. You're in a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, and in the kitchen at the back someone is already handing you a plate. This week is different. Every other door on this app spent its first camp teaching its own first words. Now you get to visit, one house a day. A guest has one simple rule: listen to how they say it, in their words, and don't take it home and blend it into yours.
screen: `FIRST DOOR: A GURDWARA.` → `ONE HOUSE A DAY.` → `LISTEN IN THEIR WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sit down on the floor, in a row, next to whoever's there. This is the langar, the free kitchen, open to anyone of any faith or none. Sikhs trace it to Guru Nanak, the first Guru, and they tell a story about the third, Guru Amar Das. He asked everyone who came to see him to eat in the langar first, in the same rows. Then the emperor Akbar came to visit, the most powerful man in India. Tradition says there was no private table for him. He sat on the floor with everyone else, ate, and only then met the Guru. Everyone at the same height. That's the first thing seva means in a Sikh home: service that erases rank, in a world where caste often decided who could eat beside whom. The second: it takes your whole self. Sikhs speak of seva with the body, cooking, sweeping, minding the shoes; with the mind; and with what you have. The third: it has no bill. In the Sukhmani, a long hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in effect, that the one who serves without wanting anything back reaches the Master. For Sikhs, seva is remembering God with your hands. Now, from your own door. You met seva on day fifteen, and Hindu homes keep an old Sanskrit line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. Feeding whoever comes isn't foreign to you. The honest difference: a Hindu host honors the guest as God; in the langar, the row itself is the teaching. Host, guest and emperor, one floor.
screen: `THE LANGAR: FREE, TO ANYONE.` · `EVERYONE AT THE SAME HEIGHT.` · `BODY, MIND AND WHAT YOU HAVE.` · `SERVICE WITH NO BILL.` · then, large: `SEVA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next meal you'll share, at home, at school, at work. Picture everyone at it sitting in one row on one floor, nobody at the head of the table. Then think of one plate you could hand to someone this week, with no bill attached. If you pray, you can offer the food first, the way many Hindu homes do.
Seva, selfless service, as Sikhs say it: a kitchen floor where everyone eats at the same height, with your whole self, and no bill attached.

324.title: The Buddha lets the breath be
324.hook: the second visit: a man who once tried to stop his breath, and learned to simply know it
324.carry: anapanasati: know the breath, don't steer it
324.howItsDone: Many Buddhists, in Theravada, Zen and Tibetan communities alike, practice mindfulness of breathing, sitting quietly and knowing each breath as it comes and goes, often in a hall with a bell to begin and end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first house: a Sikh kitchen, and seva, everyone eats at the same height. Today, a second house.

Before he was the Buddha, he was a prince who left everything to find the end of suffering. For years he pushed his body as hard as a body can be pushed. In the old Pali texts he tells it himself. He tried stopping his breath, through mouth and nose, until his head pounded as if it were being split. He ate so little that, touching his belly, he could feel his spine. None of it worked. And then, he says, he remembered a day from his childhood: sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father worked, calm and happy, without trying at all. Could that be the way?
screen: `HE TRIED TO STOP HIS BREATH.` → `IT DIDN'T WORK.` → `A ROSE-APPLE TREE, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: So he ate again, and his five companions walked off, sure he'd given up. He hadn't. He sat down and turned to the breath, not to force it but to know it. Elsewhere he says that before his awakening, this was how he mostly dwelt. The practice Buddhists keep from his teaching is called anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, and a discourse of that name lays it out almost like stage directions. Go to the forest, the root of a tree, an empty hut. Sit, legs crossed, back straight. Mindful, breathe in. Mindful, breathe out. Breathing in long, know: I breathe in long. Breathing in short, know: I breathe in short. That's the first surprise: nothing is being fixed. Many teachers point out the turn: the man who once tried to stop his breath now simply knows it. The second surprise is how far it goes. The discourse lays out sixteen steps, from the length of the breath, through the body calming, then feelings, then the mind itself, to watching everything change and letting go. And why the breath? Because it's always here, and it never stays. Buddhists call that anicca, impermanence, and the breath teaches it every few seconds. Now, from your own door. You may know pranayama from a yoga class: an old Hindu practice where the breath is counted, held and lengthened on purpose. That's a real path, and it's a different one. In the Buddha's hall, you don't steer the breath. You know it.
screen: `HE ATE AGAIN. HIS FRIENDS LEFT.` · `MINDFUL, HE BREATHES IN.` · `KNOWING, NOT STEERING.` · `SIXTEEN STEPS, ONE BREATH.` · `PRANAYAMA STEERS; THIS KNOWS.` · then, large: `ANAPANASATI.`

segments.voice: Sit, back straight, the way the text describes, and don't change the breath: when it comes in long, know it's long; when it comes in short, know it's short. When your mind wanders off, and it will, notice that too, and come back to the next breath. No counting, no holding, no goal: just a guest sitting quietly in someone else's hall.
Anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing in and out. Not steering it; knowing it, and watching it change.

325.title: Bilal on the hot sand
325.hook: the third visit: a man on burning sand saying one word, and a circle that still remembers
325.carry: dhikr: the heart coming back to God's name
325.howItsDone: Muslims do dhikr alone, often after the daily prayers on fingers or prayer beads; Sufi orders also gather in circles to repeat a phrase such as la ilaha illallah together, and the Mevlevi order performs a turning ceremony. Many Hindus do japa, repeating a name of God on a mala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anapanasati: know the breath, don't steer it. Today, a third house.

Mecca, in the first years of Islam. Bilal is an enslaved man of Ethiopian family, and he has become a Muslim. His master, Umayya, is furious. The early biographies of the Prophet tell it plainly: in the midday heat, Umayya has him laid on his back on the burning sand with a heavy rock on his chest, and orders him to give up the one God. Bilal answers with one word, again and again. Ahad. Ahad. One. One. He was later freed, and the Prophet chose him to give the call to prayer. Muslim families still tell his story to their children.

The Arabic word for keeping God's name on your lips like that is dhikr. It means remembering, and also mentioning: saying the name out loud. It belongs to all Muslims: someone who whispers subhanallah or alhamdulillah after prayer is doing dhikr. The Qur'an puts it simply. In Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Sufis are Muslims who give their lives to that line. Sufism isn't a separate religion; it's a path inside Islam, with teachers, lineages and circles, often called orders. Many gather to repeat a phrase like la ilaha illallah, there is no god but God, again and again, sometimes aloud, sometimes silently in the heart. The Mevlevi order, founded after the poet Rumi, turns remembrance into a slow turning dance. Why repeat? A Sufi would say: because the heart forgets, not out of wickedness, just busyness, and dhikr polishes it the way you'd polish a mirror. Muslims don't all agree about every Sufi practice; some question the music or the dancing. Now, from your own door. A Hindu grandmother counting a mala, Ram, Ram, is doing japa, repeating the name, and many Hindu teachers say the name carries the one it names. So the circle may feel familiar. The honest difference: dhikr remembers one God, Allah, with no image and no partner. That's the heart of Bilal's word. Japa usually calls God by a beloved name and form: Rama, Krishna, Shiva, the Mother.

segments.voice: You're a guest in the circle, so no one expects you to say their words. If you keep a mala, let one name you already love ride quietly on the breath, bead by bead. If you don't pray, just notice how often the mind wanders off, and come back to the breath each time; that coming back is the movement a Sufi calls remembering. If you are a Muslim, let a phrase you already say ride on the breath.
Dhikr, remembrance: the heart coming back to God's name, again and again.

326.title: A palace in time
326.hook: the fourth visit: a Friday table, two candles, and a day that stops the week
326.carry: shabbat: a day made holy by stopping
326.tomorrow: guided visits: what a Christian means by grace
326.howItsDone: Jews welcome Shabbat at sundown on Friday by lighting candles and blessing wine and bread, rest through Saturday with prayer, meals and family, and close it at nightfall with havdalah; how strictly work is set aside differs among Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and other Jews.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhikr: the heart coming back to God's name, and Bilal's one word. Today, a fourth house.

Friday, just before sunset. A kitchen that's been busy all afternoon goes suddenly still. The table has a white cloth, two braided loaves under a cover, a cup of wine or grape juice. Someone strikes a match and lights two candles, then draws her hands in toward her face and covers her eyes. Phones go face down, or away entirely, until Saturday night. From here to nightfall tomorrow, this house is keeping a day the Torah sets apart on its first page. Today, what a Jew means by Shabbat.
screen: `FRIDAY, JUST BEFORE SUNSET.` → `TWO CANDLES, TWO LOAVES.` → `WHAT A JEW MEANS BY SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root that means to stop, to cease. It begins on the first page of the Torah. After six days of making the world, the text says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel pointed out that the first thing the Bible makes holy isn't a place or a person. It's a day. Later, the Ten Commandments give Shabbat twice, with two different verbs. In Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy: observe it. Jewish tradition says God spoke both words at once, and some families say that's why there are two candles. Remember is the inside of the day: rest, blessing, the meal, the singing. Observe is the outside: the work you set down. Orthodox Jews refrain from thirty-nine kinds of creative work the rabbis listed; many Jews keep the day in other ways. What they share is the stop. Heschel called Shabbat a palace built in time rather than space. And it ends with a flame, a braided candle at Saturday nightfall and a blessing called havdalah, separation. Now, from your own door. Hindus have no weekly day of rest kept by everyone. Hindu holy time follows the moon instead: ekadashi fasts twice a month, festivals, a weekday some families keep for Shiva or Hanuman. The honest difference: on Shabbat, a whole people stops together, every seventh day, because the Torah's first page made a day holy.

segments.voice: Put the phone face down or out of reach, and let your hands be still, the way they'd be once a candle is lit. Let the list of unfinished things stay unfinished; it will still be there later. Breathe in: stop; breathe out: rest, a guest keeping quiet at someone else's table while they keep their day.
Shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, the seventh day made holy.

327.title: Amazing grace
327.hook: the fifth visit: a song everyone knows, written by a man who didn't think he deserved to sing it
327.howItsDone: Christians speak of grace in sermons, hymns and prayers, and many say grace before meals; Catholic and Orthodox Christians receive grace especially through the sacraments, while many Protestants emphasize grace received through faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday's house kept Shabbat: shabbat: a day made holy by stopping. Today, a fifth house.

A church, any church: stone or strip mall, a choir or a guitar. Sooner or later someone starts a song that long ago walked out of church and into the wider world. Amazing grace, how sweet the sound. It was published in England in 1779, by John Newton, a clergyman who had once worked in the Atlantic slave trade, and who later, publicly, turned against it. When he wrote about a grace that saved a wretch, he wasn't being modest. He meant it. Today, what a Christian means by grace.
screen: `A SONG THAT LEFT THE CHURCH.` → `JOHN NEWTON, 1779.` → `WHAT A CHRISTIAN MEANS BY GRACE.`

segments.voice: The New Testament's word is Greek: charis. It means a gift, a favor, something given freely. So first, grace is a gift you didn't earn. Paul puts it plainly in his letter to the Ephesians. In the King James Version: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Not a wage. A gift. Second, grace finds people at their weakest, not their best. Paul writes that he begged the Lord three times to take away something he calls a thorn in the flesh, and heard this answer: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." That's why Newton could sing it. Grace, for Christians, isn't a prize for the ones who got it right. It's what meets the ones who didn't. Third, Christians differ on how grace works, and they say so. Catholic and Orthodox Christians teach that grace comes especially through the sacraments, like baptism and communion, and that a person freely cooperates with it. Many Protestants stress grace alone: God's gift, received by faith, with good works flowing from it rather than earning it. Now, from your own door. Hindus have words for this too. Kripa is grace, and the sweet you're handed at the temple is prasad, which also means grace, a favor freely given. Krishna himself speaks of devotees reaching him by his grace. The honest difference: for Christians, grace comes through Jesus Christ, his life, his death and his rising. That's the center of their house.
screen: `CHARIS: A GIFT, FREELY GIVEN.` · `NOT A WAGE.` · `STRENGTH MADE PERFECT IN WEAKNESS.` · `CHURCHES DIFFER ON HOW IT WORKS.` · `KRIPA, PRASAD: A COUSIN.` · then, large: `GRACE.`

328.title: The thread on your wrist
328.hook: a coworker asks about the red thread on your wrist, and the demon king its verse remembers
328.carry: raksha: a thread that asks God to protect you
328.howItsDone: Many priests tie a red and yellow kalava thread on the wrist at the end of a puja, often saying a verse that names King Bali; many families put a small dot of kajal on a baby against nazar, the evil eye, and some shops hang a lemon and seven green chilies by the door.

segments.voice: Yesterday's house spoke of grace, charis: love you didn't earn. Today the visits turn around: for two days, the questions neighbors ask about your house.

A coworker notices it while you're both waiting for coffee: a red and yellow thread, a little faded, tied around your wrist. Is that a friendship bracelet? Not quite. A priest tied it at a puja weeks ago, and while he tied it he said a short Sanskrit verse. The verse names a king. His name was Bali. He was a demon king, he had conquered heaven itself, and he was famous for one thing: he never refused anyone a gift.
screen: `A RED AND YELLOW THREAD.` → `A VERSE, SAID AS IT'S TIED.` → `IT NAMES A DEMON KING.`

segments.voice: Here's his story, as the Bhagavata tells it. The gods had lost heaven to Bali, so Vishnu came to his sacrifice as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked for a gift: just three steps of land. Bali's own teacher warned him it was a trick. Bali gave anyway. A promise is a promise. Then the small boy grew until one step covered the earth and the next the heavens. No room was left for a third. So Bali bowed and offered his own head. He was bound, and he lost his kingdom. But the story doesn't end there. Vishnu, moved by a king who kept his word, gave him a world of his own and promised to stay near him and protect him. Many families hear the verse this way: the one who was bound became the one God guards. That's the verse at your wrist. As the priest ties the kalava, a raksha sutra, a protection thread, he says, in effect: with the thread that bound mighty Bali, I bind you; protection, hold firm. Raksha means protection. The thread is a prayer, tied on, asking God to look after you. The black dot on a baby's cheek is a cousin: kajal against nazar, the evil eye, the fear that even loving admiration can harm something new, so a small flaw goes on purpose. That one's a folk custom, not scripture; families keep it seriously, with a smile, or not at all. Your coffee-line answer: it's a protection thread. Someone tied it on me with a prayer.
screen: `VAMANA ASKS FOR THREE STEPS.` · `BALI KEEPS HIS WORD.` · `BOUND, THEN GUARDED BY GOD.` · `KALAVA — A RAKSHA SUTRA.` · `KAJAL AGAINST NAZAR.` · then, large: `RAKSHA.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on your wrist, as if a thread were tied there, and think of someone who has looked out for you, out loud or quietly: tied a thread, said a prayer, waited up until you got home. Let the feeling sit on your skin for a few breaths. If you pray, ask God's protection over them, the way the priest asked it over you; if you don't, simply send them your thanks.
Nazar. A look: the evil eye that families ward off with a black dot. The thread asks for raksha; the dot keeps off nazar. Today's word.
Your line: raksha, a thread that asks God to protect you. Bound like Bali, and guarded like him. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

329.title: When someone is unkind
329.hook: a stranger on a late train says she doesn't belong; Arjuna shaking in his chariot; the raised hand on the murtis
329.carry: your worth isn't up for a vote: abhaya, no fear
329.howItsDone: Many murtis of Ganesha, Durga, Vishnu and Shiva show one hand raised, palm out, in the abhaya mudra, the gesture of 'do not fear'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nazar, and the thread on your wrist: raksha, a thread that asks God to protect you. Today, the harder question: when the look isn't kind.
screen: `RAKSHA — A THREAD THAT ASKS FOR PROTECTION.`

segments.voice: She was born in this city. She went to school here, works here, loves it. One evening on a late train, a stranger tells her she doesn't really belong here, and throws in a slur meant for a religion that isn't even hers. Then he gets off at the next stop. She sits there shaking, the train still moving, everyone looking at their phones. A lot of people know a version of that night. Today, the hard part of a week about neighbors: when one isn't kind.
screen: `A LATE TRAIN.` → `YOU DON'T BELONG HERE.` → `WHEN A NEIGHBOR ISN'T KIND.`

segments.voice: She isn't the first to sit down shaking. The Gita opens with a man doing exactly that. Arjuna, the great archer, stands in his chariot between two armies, looks across, and falls apart: his limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his bow slips from his hand, and he sinks down onto the seat. After one sharp word to stand up, Krishna's answer isn't a plan. It's about who Arjuna is. The self, he says: weapons can't cut it, fire can't burn it. You met it as the atman on day eight. A stranger's words can shake you. They can't reach that. Much later, Krishna lists the qualities of a godly person, and the very first is abhaya: fearlessness. You can see it on almost any shrine. Ganesha, Durga, Vishnu, one hand raised, palm out. That's the abhaya mudra. It says: don't be afraid. So here's what the tradition puts in that hand. Your worth isn't up for a vote. Dignity, not hate: ahimsa, from day fifteen, is on Krishna's list too, and here it means not answering cruelty with cruelty. It never means staying silent or unsafe. Move away. Tell someone. Report it. Ask for help. And you're not alone. If you're ever in danger, call local emergency services. If a night like that leaves you somewhere dark, in the US you can call or text 988, any hour, and talk to someone; elsewhere, local emergency help is there too. This week you visited five houses. The bow from day four still holds, even when someone doesn't bow back.
screen: `ARJUNA SITS DOWN, SHAKING.` · `NO WEAPON CUTS THE SELF.` · `FIRST ON THE LIST: ABHAYA.` · `DIGNITY, NOT HATE.` · `YOU'RE NOT ALONE. US: CALL OR TEXT 988.` · then, large: `ABHAYA.`

segments.voice: If you like, lift your right hand, palm out, the way the murtis do, and name a moment someone made you feel small, without reliving it. Breathe in slowly, and on the out-breath let the hand say what it says: don't be afraid. If you pray, you can ask for courage; if you don't, let the steady breath be the answer. Lower your hand when you're ready.
Abhaya mudra. The raised open palm on so many murtis: no fear, don't be afraid. Today's word.
Your line: your worth isn't up for a vote. Abhaya, no fear. Nobody on a train gets to decide it. See you tomorrow.
